Identifying Risk Factors and Vulnerabilities (Part 2)

Risk factors of material, software, organizational and human resources — and how to extract them from internal reports

Thursday, November 12, 2026 · 6:00 – 10:00 pm · Online420-1C2-DW Threats and Risks · AEC (Attestation d'études collégiales) LEA.D8Topic 4 — Part 2Competency EZ02 — element 3, criteria 3.3 and 3.4Hour 1 — lecture in four lessons (60 min) · workshop in Hours 2 and 3

Good evening. On Monday you wrote the midterm; tonight we return to Kalmia and finish Topic 4.

In Class 6 you produced three lists: 24 network-architecture risk factors (the NA- rows), 34 software findings (the SW- rows) and 16 actions from the vulnerability scan (the VS- rows). All three describe technology. Tonight we add what a technical list cannot show: the condition of the equipment, the rules and contracts of the company, and the people who run it. We also learn to read the documents in which these facts are written — penetration test reports, compliance reports, incident reports, network and host monitoring reports, policies and standards.

At the end of the hour your team will hold one consolidated list of Kalmia's risk factors. On Saturday, Lab 3 starts from that list: every row will receive a likelihood and an impact.

The one fact to remember tonight

A risk factor is a fact about the organization, written with its evidence. Every row you write tonight names the asset, the condition, and the document — with its location — that proves it.

Professor cue Say the one fact out loud and leave it on the screen corner all hour. Remind the class that tonight's documents are confidential course findings and entirely fictional, and that nothing is scanned or tested tonight: we read reports.

Kalmia in one paragraph (reminder)

Torréfaction Kalmia inc. — Kalmia Coffee Roasters Inc. — is a fictional coffee roaster: roastery, office and warehouse in Saint-Laurent (Montréal), three cafés (Plateau-Mont-Royal, Old Montréal, Laval), 46 employees and about $6.8 million of revenue. Nadia Roy is President and CEO (chief executive officer) and the risk owner; Karim Haddad runs operations; Sophie Tremblay runs finance and HR (human resources); Lucas Martin is the half-time IT (information technology) coordinator. InfoNord MSP (managed service provider) manages the firewall FW-HQ, patches 'the server' and runs the helpdesk. Recorded incidents: INC-01 (March, web shop down six hours), INC-02 (June, fake banking details, $18,400 stopped by a call-back), INC-03 (August, two-hour point-of-sale outage), INC-04 (September, export of 18,500 loyalty records by a former supervisor's account), INC-05 (September, phishing text messages to baristas).

In Class 6 you produced the NA-, SW- and VS- rows. Tonight's outputs join them: resource_risk_factors.csv (Example 1), source_register.csv (Example 2), pt_risk_factors.csv (Example 3) and the consolidated list (Example 4).

Lesson 1 — Risk factors of material, software, organizational and human resources

What a risk factor is, the four resource categories, the classification rule and the cause chain
0:04 – 0:20

Read-aloud script — about 13 minutes

Professor cue Sixteen minutes. Start from Nadia Roy's question ('our scans say our problems are software — is that true?') and come back to it at the end of Example 1. Insist on the rule 'what must change?' and on one condition per row; the closet example (human row + organizational row) is the one students remember.

From a list of weaknesses to a list of risk factors

Until now we have collected weaknesses one family at a time: the network in Class 6, the software in Class 6, the scan report in Class 6. Tonight we change the question. We no longer ask 'what is broken in this system?' but 'what, inside Kalmia, makes harm more likely or more serious?' The answer is a list of risk factors.

NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-30 Rev. 1, the guide we have used since Class 1, defines a risk factor as 'a characteristic used in a risk model as an input to determining the level of risk in a risk assessment' (NIST glossary). The guide names five typical risk factors: the threat, the vulnerability, the impact, the likelihood and the predisposing condition. Lab 2 covers the threats; Topic 5 will cover likelihood and impact. Tonight covers the two risk factors that live inside the organization: vulnerabilities and predisposing conditions.

Vulnerability and predisposing condition

A vulnerability is a weakness in an information system, in its security procedures, in its internal controls or in their implementation, that a threat source could exploit or trigger. Note that the definition is not limited to software: a missing procedure or an internal control that is not applied is also a vulnerability.

A predisposing condition is a condition that exists within an organization, a business process, its architecture or an information system and its environment, and that increases or decreases the likelihood that a threat event, once started, results in harm (NIST glossary). A predisposing condition is not a flaw that someone exploits directly; it is a property that makes every flaw more or less dangerous.

Kalmia gives one example of each. The NAS-01 administrator password stored in a file readable by all staff is a vulnerability: an attacker who reads the file uses it. The flat head-office network is a predisposing condition: no attacker 'exploits' a flat network, but on a flat network any compromised device can reach NAS-01, so every other weakness becomes more likely to cause harm.

Why four resource categories

The competency EZ02 (criterion 3.3) asks for the main risk factors associated with four groups of resources — the means an organization uses to operate: material resources, software, organizational resources and human resources.

The four categories serve two purposes. The first is completeness. A list built only from scans and inventories contains almost nothing but software rows, because scanners see programs and ports. The categories force the analyst to look in the four places where weaknesses exist. The second purpose comes in Topic 6: each category tends to call a different type of control. Material factors usually call physical controls, software factors technical controls, organizational factors administrative controls, and human factors training and supervision.

ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27005 uses the same idea: in its annex on risk assessment techniques, the examples of typical vulnerabilities are grouped by the type of asset that carries them — hardware, software, network, personnel, site and organization. Our four categories group those six: hardware and site are material; software and the configuration of network devices are software; organization is organizational; personnel is human.

Material resources

Material resources are the physical items and places the organization depends on: computers, servers, storage, network devices, payment terminals, power equipment, cabling, portable devices, removable media, and the rooms that contain them.

  • Age and support: hardware past its end of support, or with no spare parts.
  • Signs of failure: disk warnings, battery tests, temperature alarms.
  • Single points of failure: one disk without a spare, one internet link, one power supply.
  • Environment: heat, dust, water, unstable power.
  • Physical protection: locks, cabinets, access to rooms — the lock itself is material; leaving it open is human.
  • Portable and unauthorized devices: laptops that can be lost or stolen, a consumer Wi-Fi extender plugged in by an employee.

At Kalmia: disk 3 of NAS-01 reports 48 reallocated sectors and the count is rising; the UPS-HQ battery gives four minutes of runtime when fifteen are needed for a clean shutdown; the server closet has no ventilation and NAS-01 reached 58 degrees Celsius on October 9; each café has one internet link and no backup link. None of these appears in a vulnerability scan. They appear in monitoring reports and incident reports — the subject of Lesson 2.

Software

Software includes operating systems, applications, firmware, cloud services and their configuration. We place configuration in the software category because a configuration is a set of values stored in a program or in a device: changing it is a change to software, even when no new version is installed.

  • End of support and missing patches (Class 6).
  • Insecure configuration: default or shared credentials, clear-text administration, unnecessary services.
  • Missing security functions: no MFA (multi-factor authentication), no lockout, no logging.
  • Unknown versions: a version nobody can name is a finding in itself.

Kalmia's Class 6 lists are mostly software rows, and they stay in the list. Tonight adds a few that only internal sources reveal: legacy authentication (IMAP [Internet Message Access Protocol]) still enabled on the shared mailbox commandes@ (monitoring report MR-02), and MFA enforced on 2 of 31 Microsoft 365 accounts.

Organizational resources

Organizational resources are the way the company is organized to protect itself: its roles and responsibilities, its processes, its policies, procedures and standards, its contracts with suppliers, its budget and its documentation.

  • A policy or a procedure that is missing, outdated, never approved or not applied.
  • A responsibility that nobody holds.
  • A contract that leaves a gap between the supplier and the client.
  • No periodic review (accounts, permissions, backups, findings).
  • Declarations to third parties that do not match reality.
  • A legal obligation that is not met.

At Kalmia: there is no incident response plan; there is no offboarding procedure, which allowed a former supervisor's account to export 18,500 loyalty records (INC-04); the InfoNord contract covers 'the server and the firewall', so NAS-01 and the cameras have no patch owner; the backup procedure is a 2023 draft that was never approved. The absence of a document is evidence when the person who should know confirms it in writing — here, Nadia Roy's list of existing documents, sent on November 6.

Human resources

Human resources are the people of the organization considered from the point of view of security: what they know, what they do, and how many of them are available to do what is needed.

  • Knowledge: awareness of phishing and fraud, measured for example by a phishing simulation.
  • Behaviour: shared passwords, passwords written down or stored in files, visitors let in without question.
  • Availability: one person who knows everything (a key-person dependency), workload, high turnover.
  • Insiders: current or former staff who keep access they no longer need.

At Kalmia: 9 of 30 staff entered their password in the May phishing simulation and only 2 reported it; one NAS (network-attached storage) administrator password is shared by four people; one half-time IT (information technology) coordinator holds all the network knowledge; café turnover is about 40 per cent a year.

One rule of professional ethics applies here. A human risk factor describes a condition of a role or a group, never a person to blame. We write 'the shared Administrator account of the web shop is used by two marketing employees', not the names of the employees. A risk analysis names conditions so that they can be treated; it is not an investigation of individuals.

The classification rule: what must change?

Students hesitate between categories because one situation often touches several. Use one question: what must change to remove this condition?

  • A physical item must be repaired, replaced or added → material.
  • A program, firmware or a setting must change → software.
  • A rule, a document, a role, a contract or a process must be created, approved or applied → organizational.
  • What people know, what they do, or how many of them are available must change → human.

One row holds one condition. When two different things must change, write two rows and link them. 'The server closet was unlocked with the key in the door' is a human row: the lock works, people leave it open. 'The closet is left unlocked so that the cleaning staff can enter' is an organizational row: management decided it. Both are true, both are needed, and they are treated differently.

One observation, several faces: the cause chain

A technical weakness usually has an organizational cause, and the organizational cause often has a human one. We call this sequence the cause chain. Take NAS-01: its firmware has not been updated for 900 days (software). Why? The InfoNord contract covers 'the server and the firewall' and nobody decided whether NAS-01 is 'the server' (organizational). Why was the gap not noticed? The only person who could notice is a half-time IT coordinator with no time left for it (human).

Writing the three rows matters because their treatments differ: an update, a contract amendment, and a second trained person. A list that keeps only the technical row leads to installing the update while the next update is missed for the same reason. The same logic applies to INC-04: the export of 18,500 records was the incident; the missing offboarding procedure is the risk factor that allowed it, and it is still present tonight.

This is why Example 1 below does more than sort rows. It also draws the links between them.

Key terms of this lesson

Risk factor
A characteristic used in a risk model as an input to determining the level of risk (NIST [National Institute of Standards and Technology] SP [Special Publication] 800-30 Rev. 1): threat, vulnerability, impact, likelihood, predisposing condition.
Vulnerability
A weakness in a system, its security procedures, internal controls or implementation that a threat source could exploit or trigger.
Predisposing condition
A condition of the organization, a process, the architecture or a system and its environment that increases or decreases the likelihood that a threat event results in harm.
Material resources
Physical items and places: computers, servers, network devices, payment terminals, power equipment, portable devices, rooms.
Software
Operating systems, applications, firmware, cloud services and their configuration.
Organizational resources
Roles, processes, policies, procedures, standards, contracts, budget and documentation.
Human resources
People considered for their knowledge, their behaviour and their availability.
Key-person dependency
A situation in which one person holds knowledge or access that nobody else has.
Cause chain
The link from a technical weakness to its organizational cause and, often, to a human cause.
Micro-activity — classify five facts (3 min)

Use the question 'what must change?' to classify each fact: (a) the UPS-HQ battery gives 4 minutes of runtime; (b) the InfoNord contract excludes 'equipment supplied by third parties'; (c) 9 of 30 staff entered their password in the phishing simulation; (d) legacy authentication (IMAP [Internet Message Access Protocol]) is enabled on commandes@; (e) the server closet was unlocked with the key in the door.

(a) Material — the battery must be replaced. (b) Organizational — the contract must change. (c) Human — what people know and do must change (the missing training programme is a separate organizational row). (d) Software — a setting must change. (e) Human — the lock works, people leave it open; the decision to leave it open for the cleaners is a second, organizational row. Correct the frequent error 'a physical problem is always material'.

Real-life example — Kalmia's observations sorted into four resource categories, with their cause chains

The task of this example

From 23 observations collected in the evidence pack (monitoring reports, incident reports, the penetration test, policies and an interview), decide for each one what must change, place it in its resource category, reject what is not evidence, and draw the cause chains between rows.

How it relates to this lecture

This is Lesson 1 applied to the case: the four categories of criterion 3.3, the 'what must change?' rule, the 'one condition per row' rule and the cause chain.

Where it goes next (future labs)

Class 9 workshop (the 22 accepted rows are the category starting list of the team list); Lab 3 — Risk register and prioritization (each register row carries its category, starting Saturday, November 14); Lab 4 — Risk treatment and prevention plan (the category guides the type of control: physical, technical or administrative).

The answer to Nadia Roy is no. Eight of the 22 accepted rows are organizational — more than any other category — and none of them could appear in a scan. Five cause chains link the categories: for example, the contract gap (organizational) explains the NAS-01 firmware (software), and the missing awareness programme (organizational) explains the phishing result (human).

Code example 1 (Python) — Classify Kalmia's observations by resource category

The task of this code

A Python script that reads observations.csv (23 rows), applies the 'what must change?' rule to each row, rejects rows without a source, prints every decision with its justification, draws the cause chains declared between rows, counts the rows per category and writes resource_risk_factors.csv.

How it relates to the lecture and to the real-life example

The script performs Example 1 exactly as Lesson 1 describes it: the rule is a table that anyone can read, every decision is printed, and a row without evidence is rejected. The visualization places each row in its quadrant and draws the chains, so the class sees the cause chain appear.

kalmia_resource_classifier.pystep 0
Execution window — the recorded output, step by step (pause to discuss a step)

The steps replayed above are the real output of the script, recorded when it was run on the course data on November 10, 2026 (Python 3 / PowerShell 7.4). Run it yourself from the downloaded folder to obtain the same result.

Step by step — what the code does

  1. The script imports the csv module and defines FIX_TO_CATEGORY, a dictionary that is the classification rule of Lesson 1: each value of the column fix_target (device, firmware, contract, behaviour…) is mapped to one category.
  2. read_rows() opens a CSV (comma-separated values) file with the encoding utf-8-sig (which also accepts files saved by Excel) and returns a list of dictionaries, one per row, whose keys are the column names.
  3. main() reads observations.csv and prints [LOAD] with the number of rows, then prints the rule once, so that each decision can be checked against it.
  4. The first loop examines each observation. A row with an empty source is rejected with [REJECT]: without a source it is an opinion. A row whose fix target is not in the rule is also rejected, so that a person classifies it by hand.
  5. For every accepted row, the category is looked up in the dictionary, the counter of that category is increased, the row is stored, and an [OBS] line prints the asset, the fix target, the category and the source.
  6. The second loop reads the column causes. For each identifier listed there, an [CHAIN] line prints the cause and its category, then the effect and its category — for example OBS-12 (organizational) → OBS-06 (software).
  7. A [COUNT] line prints the four counters and the number of rejected rows: 4 material, 5 software, 8 organizational, 5 human, 1 rejected.
  8. The accepted rows are written to resource_risk_factors.csv with the columns id, category, asset, risk_factor, source and causes, and a [WRITE] line confirms the file. That file is the category starting list of the workshop.

Self-check — 4 MCQs and 2 MSQs

Formative self-check — not evaluated. Quiz 3 (Monday, November 16) is a separate, evaluated quiz.
1. In NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-30 Rev. 1, which of the following is a predisposing condition rather than a vulnerability? (MCQ — one answer)
  • ✕ This is a vulnerability: the default password is used directly to log in.
  • ✕ This is a vulnerability: it allows password guessing directly.
  • ✕ This is a vulnerability: an attacker reads the file and uses the password directly.
  • ✓ Correct. Nobody exploits a flat network directly, but it makes every compromised device able to reach NAS-01: it increases the likelihood that a threat event causes harm.
💡 Hint: A predisposing condition is a property that makes other weaknesses more or less dangerous; nobody exploits it directly.
2. Using the rule 'what must change?', in which category does 'the InfoNord contract covers only the server and the firewall' belong? (MCQ — one answer)
  • ✕ The consequence (unpatched firmware) is a software row, but the contract itself is not software.
  • ✕ No one's knowledge or behaviour must change to fix the contract; it is a document agreed between two companies.
  • ✓ Correct. A contract is an organizational resource: the contract (or an amendment) must change.
  • ✕ No physical item must change.
💡 Hint: Ask what must be rewritten to remove the gap.
3. The server closet was found unlocked with the key in the door. The lock works. What is the correct classification of this observation? (MCQ — one answer)
  • ✕ There is no program or setting involved.
  • ✕ A physical-security observation is material only when a physical item must be repaired, replaced or added.
  • ✓ Correct. The lock works, so nothing material must change; what people do must change. The management decision is a separate organizational row.
  • ✕ A risk factor is a condition, not an incident; the condition exists whether or not something was stolen.
💡 Hint: The lock is a material item; ask whether the lock must be repaired.
4. Why does the competency ask for risk factors in four resource categories instead of one list built from the scans? (MCQ — one answer)
  • ✕ Likelihood is assessed in Topic 5 with one scale for all rows.
  • ✕ All findings are confidential (Legal Notice, s. 7.5).
  • ✕ The categories classify internal conditions; threats are a separate risk factor.
  • ✓ Correct. Completeness is the first purpose; the second is that each category tends to call a different type of control in Topic 6.
💡 Hint: Think about what a scanner can see.
5. Which of the following are human risk factors at Kalmia? (MSQ — select 3 answers)
  • ✓ Knowledge and behaviour of people — human.
  • ✓ Availability of people (key-person dependency) — human.
  • ✕ A document that is not approved — organizational.
  • ✕ A physical item that must be replaced — material.
  • ✓ A practice of people — human.
  • ✕ A setting — software.
💡 Hint: Human = what people know, what they do, or how many are available.
6. Which statements about the cause chain are correct? (MSQ — select 3 answers)
  • ✓ This is the definition used in Lesson 1.
  • ✓ One condition per row; the link keeps the relationship visible.
  • ✕ Every row still needs its own evidence.
  • ✓ The NAS-01 update would be installed, and the next one missed for the same reason.
  • ✕ Human risk factors describe roles and groups, never a person to blame.
  • ✕ All links are kept; their treatments differ.
💡 Hint: The chain links rows; it does not merge them or rank them.

Lesson 2 — Internal information sources

Penetration test reports, compliance reports, incident reports, network and host monitoring reports, policies and standards
0:20 – 0:36

Read-aloud script — about 13 minutes

Professor cue Sixteen minutes, five sources, three minutes each. For every source ask the same two questions: what can it reveal, and what can it not reveal? End with the five questions for judging a source — Example 2 applies them.

Internal and public information sources

In Class 5 you used public information sources — newsletters, advisories, CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) records, MITRE ATT&CK — to learn what attackers do in general. Internal information sources tell you what is true inside one organization: which weaknesses exist, which ones were exploited, which rules exist and which are applied.

The competency EZ02 lists them in its achievement context: besides the asset inventory, penetration test reports, compliance reports, incident reports, network and host monitoring activity reports, and policies and standards. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-30 Rev. 1 asks for the same thing in its preparation step (Task 1-4): before assessing risk, identify the sources of threat, vulnerability and impact information that the assessment will use.

Internal sources are confidential. Section 7.5 of the Legal Notice states that every finding, weakness or gap you learn about an organization stays confidential without time limit. Tonight's sixteen documents are fictional course copies; the rule still applies to the way you store and share them.

Penetration test reports (1/2) — what the report contains

A penetration test is a security test in which authorized testers imitate real attacks to find ways around the security of a system, a network, people or premises (NIST SP 800-115). Class 6 showed the difference with a vulnerability scan: a scan lists potential weaknesses automatically; a penetration test proves which ones can actually be exploited, and in what sequence.

A professional report follows a stable structure: a header (client, report identifier, dates, authorization), an executive summary for management, the scope and the method, the limitations, the findings, the positive observations, and appendices with the evidence. Each finding has an identifier, a severity, the asset, a description of the weakness, the evidence, the contributing factors and a recommendation.

A test requires a written scope and written authorization before it starts — section 7.7.2 of the Legal Notice and Annex D. Kalmia's report PT-2026-05 shows it in its header: rules of engagement signed by Nadia Roy on May 4, 2026.

Penetration test reports (2/2) — what it reveals, and what it cannot

A penetration test report reveals weaknesses that were proven exploitable, attack paths that combine several categories — a password in a file (human) plus an administration port open to all (software) — and, in the contributing factors, the organizational causes.

It cannot reveal anything outside its scope or its time window. PT-2026-05 excluded ROAST-PC and the café networks: for those, the report says nothing, and 'nothing' must be recorded as an unknown, never as 'no risk'. It describes the systems during the testing period — May 11 to 15, 2026 — so each finding must be checked against more recent evidence. Finally, the severity in the report (High, Medium, Low) is the tester's rating of the weakness; the risk level for Kalmia is decided in Topic 5 with likelihood and impact.

Compliance reports

A compliance report states, requirement by requirement, whether an organization meets a law, a regulation, a standard or a contract. It can be an internal self-assessment, an external audit, an attestation (a formal opinion signed by an auditor), or a questionnaire sent to a client or an insurer.

Two laws and standards matter for Kalmia. The first is Québec's Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector, amended by Law 25 and overseen by the CAI (Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec). It requires a person in charge of the protection of personal information whose title and contact information are published on the website (s. 3.1), governance policies (s. 3.2), a privacy impact assessment for new information system projects (s. 3.3), notice to the CAI and to the persons concerned when a confidentiality incident presents a risk of serious injury (s. 3.5), and a register of confidentiality incidents (s. 3.8). The second is PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard), which merchants accepting payment cards must meet and confirm every year, often with a self-assessment questionnaire (SAQ [Self-Assessment Questionnaire]).

Kalmia has two compliance documents. CR-2026-02 is the Law 25 self-assessment of October 16: no governance policy, the person in charge not designated in writing nor published, and the risk-of-serious-injury assessment of INC-04 not documented. CR-2026-01 is the cyber-insurance renewal questionnaire of June 20: it declares MFA (multi-factor authentication) for all remote access, offline backups and no end-of-life systems. Each nonconformity is an organizational risk factor; each declaration that other evidence contradicts is a risk factor too. Remember the limit: a self-assessment is a declaration — the weakest kind of evidence until another source confirms it.

Incident reports

An incident report records an incident: the timeline, how it was detected, its impact, the actions taken, the root cause, the contributing factors and the lessons learned. NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (April 2025) places incident response inside cybersecurity risk management: lessons learned are meant to change the organization's risk decisions.

Incident reports are strong evidence: the condition already produced harm. Read them for the condition, not for the event. The export of 18,500 loyalty records (INC-04) is the event; the account not disabled at departure, because no offboarding procedure exists, is the risk factor — and it is still present. INC-02 gives another: no written verification step for changes to supplier banking details; the $18,400 payment was stopped only by a personal habit.

Their limit is detection. An incident report exists only for what was noticed. INC-04 was found two weeks after the export, in an audit log that nobody reviewed regularly: the absence of incident reports is never proof that a risk is absent.

Network and host monitoring reports

A monitoring report is the periodic output of a tool that observes the network or the systems: a firewall report, a sign-in log, a system log, a backup job report, an endpoint protection console, a hardware or UPS (uninterruptible power supply) self-test. NIST SP 800-92 explains log management and NIST SP 800-137 describes continuous monitoring as an ongoing input to risk decisions.

Monitoring reports show current conditions that tests rarely show: an exposure confirmed by real attempts (41,870 blocked logins on the FW-HQ portal in October, MR-01), unannounced night sessions of the roaster vendor (MR-01), MFA registered on 2 of 31 accounts (MR-02), eleven failed backup nights (MR-03), a failing disk and a weak UPS battery (MR-03, MR-04), and devices that stopped reporting (MR-05).

Two limits. A tool reports only what it sees: ROAST-PC is not managed by the endpoint protection, so MR-05 says nothing about it. And a report that nobody reads protects nothing: eleven backup failures went unnoticed, which is an organizational risk factor of its own. Logs also contain personal information — section 7.2 of the Legal Notice asks you to treat them that way.

Policies and standards

A policy is a statement of management's intent and rules, approved by management. A standard sets a mandatory, measurable requirement (for example a minimum password length). A procedure gives the steps to follow, and a guideline gives advice. External references — NIST CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0, ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27001, CIS (Center for Internet Security) Controls v8.1 and the Cyber Centre's baseline controls for small and medium organizations — let you compare what a company wrote with what is expected.

Ask four questions of every policy: Does it exist? Is it approved and current? Do the people concerned know it? Is it applied — and what is the evidence? Kalmia's documents fail in four different ways. PS-01, the IT (information technology) acceptable use policy, dates from 2019 and was never revised: it still requires passwords changed every 90 days, while NIST SP 800-63B-4 now states that verifiers shall not require periodic changes, and it allows personal devices on the head-office Wi-Fi. PS-02, the backup procedure, is a draft that was never approved, and its weekly off-site copy was never made. PS-03, the InfoNord contract, leaves NAS-01 without a patch owner. And there is no incident response plan at all, although it is the first of the Cyber Centre's thirteen baseline controls.

Judging a source: five questions

Before you extract anything from a document, judge the document itself.

  1. Date — how old is it, compared with the useful life of that type of document? A monitoring report is useful for weeks, a penetration test for about a year, a policy until its review date.
  2. Scope — what does it cover, and what does it exclude?
  3. Author — internal or external, independent or not? A supplier reporting on its own service has an interest in the result.
  4. Method — how was the fact obtained? From strongest to weakest: tested, monitored, observed in an incident, documented, declared.
  5. Evidence — screenshots, logs, references: can someone else verify the fact?

Example 2 applies these five questions to the sixteen documents of the evidence pack, and shows which Kalmia assets no current source covers.

Key terms of this lesson

Internal information source
A document produced inside or for one organization that shows its actual weaknesses, incidents, controls and rules.
Penetration test
An authorized test in which testers imitate real attacks to find ways around security (NIST [National Institute of Standards and Technology] SP [Special Publication] 800-115).
Scope and limitations
What a test or an assessment covered, and what it did not cover; a limitation is recorded as an unknown.
Severity (in a report)
The author's rating of a weakness in general; not the organization's risk level.
Compliance report
A statement, requirement by requirement, of whether a law, regulation, standard or contract is met.
Attestation
A formal opinion on the results of an audit, signed by the auditor.
Root cause / contributing factor
The condition that, once removed, prevents the incident; contributing factors are other conditions that made it possible or worse.
Monitoring report
The periodic output of a tool that observes the network or the systems.
Policy, standard, procedure, guideline
Management's approved intent and rules; a mandatory measurable requirement; the steps to follow; a recommendation.

Then ask: which of the five is the weakest evidence? (b) as long as nobody checks the website — a self-assessment is a declaration.

Real-life example — Kalmia's internal source register — 16 documents judged by date, author, method and coverage

The task of this example

Read the header of each of the 16 documents of the evidence pack, judge the source with the five questions (date, scope, author, method, evidence), compute its freshness against its useful life, and map which of Kalmia's 14 critical assets each source covers and with which strength of evidence.

How it relates to this lecture

This is Lesson 2 applied to the case: the five types of internal sources, what each can and cannot reveal, and the five questions for judging a source.

Where it goes next (future labs)

Class 9 workshop (every row of the team list cites source IDs [identifier] from this register); Lab 3 — Risk register (the evidence and confidence columns of each register row); Lab 4 — Risk treatment and prevention plan (assets without current evidence call detective controls and new tests: ROAST-PC, the cafés, the loyalty console).

Lucas Martin put every report he could find in one folder named Rapports. Before anyone reads a finding, Nadia Roy wants to know which documents can be trusted, and for which assets Kalmia has no recent evidence at all.

Code example 2 (PowerShell 7) — Build Kalmia's internal source register

The task of this code

A PowerShell script that lists the report files of the folder evidence, reads the header of each one (identifier, type, author, independence, date, status, method, assets covered, exclusions), computes its age and freshness, maps each of the 14 critical assets to the sources that cover it with the strongest method, flags the coverage gaps, and exports source_register.csv and coverage_matrix.csv.

How it relates to the lecture and to the real-life example

The script applies the five questions of Lesson 2 to every document in the folder and makes the limits of each source visible. The visualization draws the age of each source against its useful life, and fills the coverage matrix cell by cell.

Build-KalmiaSourceRegister.ps1step 0
Execution window — the recorded output, step by step (pause to discuss a step)

The steps replayed above are the real output of the script, recorded when it was run on the course data on November 10, 2026 (Python 3 / PowerShell 7.4). Run it yourself from the downloaded folder to obtain the same result.

Step by step — what the code does

  1. The script fixes the reference date to November 12, 2026, loads max_age.csv into a hash table (useful life in days for each type of document) and loads assets.csv (the 14 critical assets of the Lab 1 inventory).
  2. Two small tables translate methods into strengths: tested = 5, monitored = 4, incident = 3, documented = 2, declared = 1. The strongest method available for an asset is its best evidence.
  3. Get-ChildItem lists the files of the folder evidence, sorted by name, and an [LOAD] line reports how many documents and assets were loaded.
  4. For each file, Get-Content reads the lines until the separator ---. Each 'Key: value' line is split at the first colon and stored in the hash table $Header.
  5. The age is computed by subtracting the document date from the reference date. The freshness rule gives STALE after the useful life, AGING after one third of it, otherwise CURRENT; a document whose status is Draft also receives the flag DRAFT. A [DOC] line prints the judgement.
  6. For each asset, the script looks for it in the field Covers of every source. Each match prints a [COVER] line and fills a cell of the matrix with the method; the strongest method found becomes the best evidence.
  7. The script also lists the tests that explicitly excluded the asset. An asset is a GAP when its best evidence is weaker than monitoring or when a test excluded it. An [ASSET] line prints the conclusion.
  8. Group-Object counts the sources by freshness, a [SUMMARY] line prints the counts and the number of gaps, and Export-Csv writes source_register.csv and coverage_matrix.csv.

Graph 2 — Kalmia's internal sources: age against useful life, and evidence coverage of 14 assets

Left: the age of each document compared with the useful life of its type (green = current, amber = aging, red = stale). Right: which source covers which asset, and how strongly; red rows are coverage gaps.

Self-check — 4 MCQs and 2 MSQs

1. PT-2026-05 excluded ROAST-PC at the vendor's request. How must the analyst record ROAST-PC in the risk factor list? (MCQ — one answer)
  • ✕ Leaving it out hides an unknown from the risk owner.
  • ✓ Correct. An exclusion means the testers did not look; nothing can be concluded, so the gap is recorded as an unknown.
  • ✕ Absence of findings for an excluded asset proves nothing.
  • ✕ The analyst records what is known; an exclusion is not a weakness rating.
💡 Hint: What can a report conclude about something it did not examine?
2. Under Québec's private-sector privacy law, as amended by Law 25, what must an enterprise do when a confidentiality incident presents a risk of serious injury? (MCQ — one answer)
  • ✕ The website obligation of s. 3.1 concerns the title and contact information of the person in charge.
  • ✕ That is not the obligation of section 3.5.
  • ✓ Correct. Section 3.5 requires prompt notice to the CAI (Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec) and to the persons whose information is concerned; every incident also goes into the register (s. 3.8).
  • ✕ The register is required for every incident, but a risk of serious injury also requires notification.

  • ✕ That comes from MR-04, not from the backup failures.
  • ✓ Correct. A monitoring report that nobody reads protects nothing; the missing responsibility is a risk factor of its own (KRF-21).

  • ✕ SP 800-63B-4 contains the password verifier requirements.
  • ✓ Correct. The policy is outdated: an outdated rule in a policy is an organizational risk factor.

Lesson 3 — Careful analysis: extracting risk factors from a report

Fact, inference, recommendation and limitation; the seven-step reading method; risk factor statements; corroboration and confidence
0:36 – 0:50

Read-aloud script — about 11 minutes

Professor cue Fourteen minutes. Read steps 1 and 2 on PT-2026-05 together before showing any finding. Run Code example 3 to step 6 and stop on PT-05: the conflict with the insurance questionnaire is the key teaching moment.

What 'careful analysis' means

Criterion 3.4 of the competency asks for a careful analysis of various internal sources of pertinent information. The performance criteria of the competency as a whole say what 'careful' means in practice: an accurate interpretation of the available data, the consideration and synthesis of several sources, and respect for the confidentiality of the results.

In this lesson we take one document, the penetration test report PT-2026-05, and read it with a method. The method is the same for every internal source; only the names of the sections change.

Fact, inference, recommendation, limitation

A report mixes four kinds of statements, and only one of them becomes a risk factor directly.

  • A fact is an observation with evidence that someone else can verify: 'the file acces.txt, readable by all staff, contained the administrator password' (screenshots 4 and 5). Facts become risk factors.
  • An inference is a conclusion drawn from facts: 'an attacker with a foothold on any office computer could destroy the file server and its backup'. An inference is useful context; it is verified before it is used.
  • A recommendation is a proposed action: 'create individual administrator accounts with MFA (multi-factor authentication)'. It is not a risk factor; it is kept for Lab 4.
  • A limitation is something the author did not examine: 'ROAST-PC was excluded'. It becomes an unknown.

Mixing them is the most frequent error in student lists: a recommendation written as a risk factor ('NAS-01 needs MFA') hides the condition and suggests that only one solution exists.

The seven-step reading method

  1. Identify the document — type, author, date, period, scope, authorization, classification. Compute its age.
  2. Read the limits — exclusions, time window, methods not used. Each limit becomes an unknown.
  3. Extract atomic facts — one condition per row, with its location in the document (section, finding, line).
  4. Translate each fact into a risk factor statement: asset, condition, source.
  5. Classify — resource category (Lesson 1), vulnerability or predisposing condition, and the cause chain.
  6. Corroborate — look for the same fact in another source and give it a confidence level.
  7. Record — write the row in the list with its identifier, references, confidence, business owner and open questions; store it as a confidential finding.

Steps 1 and 2 come before any finding on purpose. A reader who starts with the findings forgets to ask whether the report is old, whether it covered the system in question, and who wrote it.

Steps 1 and 2 on PT-2026-05

Step 1. PT-2026-05 was written by Nordet Sécurité, an external firm, on May 29, 2026, after testing from May 11 to 15. The rules of engagement were signed by Nadia Roy on May 4. It is classified confidential. On November 12 it is 167 days old: every finding describes May, and the November evidence — the Class 6 scan, the October monitoring reports — tells us which findings are still true.

Step 2. The report lists four limitations. ROAST-PC and the roaster controller were excluded (L-1); the café networks were not in scope (L-2); no denial-of-service test was performed (L-3); no retest was performed (L-4). They become four unknowns. L-4 also produces a risk factor of its own once we compare with November: the Internet-facing FW-HQ portal, the shared NAS (network-attached storage) administrator account and the web shop without MFA are still present six months later, and no finding has an owner or a due date (KRF-28).

Steps 3 to 5: from a finding to rows

Take finding PT-04 (physical access to the server closet). The report gives three weaknesses and two contributing factors. Step 3 extracts five atomic facts, each with its line number. Step 4 writes each one as a statement. Step 5 classifies them: the three weaknesses — visitors not challenged, the key in the door, the Wi-Fi key on a label — are human: the lock works and nothing physical is missing; people's practices must change. The two contributing factors — no visitor procedure, the closet left unlocked for the cleaning staff — are organizational: a rule must be written and a management decision changed.

Notice what is absent: PT-04 contains no material row, and the whole report contains none. A penetration test looks for exploitable weaknesses; the failing disk, the weak battery and the hot closet come from monitoring reports. This is why one source is never enough for a complete list.

Writing a risk factor statement

Use one pattern: asset or process — condition (source, location).

  • Good: 'NAS-01 — the administrator password is stored in a text file readable by all staff (PT-2026-05, PT-01, line 28)'.
  • Poor: 'NAS-01 is insecure' — no condition that anyone can verify.
  • Poor: 'NAS-01 needs MFA' — a recommendation, not a condition.
  • Poor: 'Lucas forgot to protect the NAS' — it names a person and blames; describe the condition of the role instead.
  • Poor: 'NAS-01 password in a file — high risk' — the level of risk is decided in Topic 5, not when the row is written.

Four rules follow from the examples: one condition per row; observable and verifiable; no solution inside the statement; no likelihood or impact yet.

Step 6: corroboration and confidence

Corroboration means finding the same fact in a second, independent source. The result is a confidence level written on the row.

  • CONFIRMED — at least two independent sources agree. PT-06 (portal on the Internet) is confirmed by the Class 6 network list (NA-16) and by October's 41,870 blocked login attempts (MR-01).
  • SINGLE — one source only: keep the row and ask for a second source. 'The Wi-Fi key was written on a label' rests on photographs from May; a walk-through of the closet would confirm or close it.
  • CONFLICT — sources disagree. PT-05 says the vendor's remote access has no MFA; the insurance questionnaire CR-2026-01 says MFA is required for all remote access. A conflict is never settled by choosing the source you prefer: the conflict itself is recorded as a risk factor (KRF-23), because Kalmia made a declaration to its insurer that its own evidence contradicts.
  • UNKNOWN — not examined (the limitations of step 2).

Independence matters. Two documents written by the same person from the same data count as one source. The tester's report and the firewall logs are independent: different authors, different methods.

Step 7: record — and severity is not risk

The last step writes each row with its identifier, its references (document, finding, line), its category, its confidence, its business owner and its open question. The rows of PT-2026-05 join the workshop list in Lesson 4. The positive observations of the report are recorded too, not as risk factors but as existing controls: MFA on the two administrator accounts, audit logging in Microsoft 365, the hosting company's daily backup. In Topic 5 they lower the likelihood of some risks.

Finally, do not copy the report's severity into your risk level. 'High' is the tester's rating of the weakness in general. Whether it is a high risk for Kalmia depends on the likelihood and on the impact on Kalmia's assets — the subject of Classes 10 and 11.

Key terms of this lesson

Careful analysis (criterion 3.4)
Reading internal sources with a method: accurate interpretation, synthesis of several sources, confidentiality of results.
Fact
An observation with evidence that someone else can verify; facts become risk factors.
Inference
A conclusion drawn from facts; verified before it is used.
Recommendation
A proposed action; kept for the treatment plan (Lab 4), never written as a risk factor.
Limitation
Something the author did not examine; recorded as an unknown.
Atomic fact
A statement that contains exactly one condition.
Risk factor statement
Asset or process — condition (source, location).
Corroboration
Finding the same fact in a second, independent source.
Confidence level
CONFIRMED, SINGLE, CONFLICT or UNKNOWN, written on each row.
Existing control
A protection that is already in place (a positive observation); it lowers likelihood later.
Micro-activity — fact, inference, recommendation or limitation? (3 min)

Label each sentence from PT-2026-05: (a) 'Lockout after five failed attempts is active.' (b) 'An attacker with a foothold on any office computer could destroy the file server and its backup.' (c) 'Restrict the portal to the addresses of InfoNord or to the VPN (virtual private network).' (d) 'No denial-of-service test was performed.' (e) 'The first password was entered 4 minutes after sending.'

(a) Fact — and a positive one: an existing control that lowers the likelihood of guessing the FW-HQ password. (b) Inference — derived from PT-01; verify before using. (c) Recommendation — keep for Lab 4. (d) Limitation — an unknown about availability. (e) Fact — evidence for the human row of PT-02.

Real-life example — PT-2026-05 read with the seven-step method — 27 rows from one report

The task of this example

Apply the seven steps to the penetration test report PT-2026-05: identify the report and its age, turn its four limitations into unknowns, extract its 10 weaknesses and 13 contributing factors as atomic rows with their line numbers, propose a category for each one, corroborate every row with the other Kalmia sources, and record the result.

How it relates to this lecture

This is Lesson 3 applied to one internal source: fact versus recommendation and limitation, the seven steps, the statement pattern and the confidence levels.

Where it goes next (future labs)

Class 9 workshop (the PT rows join the team list); Lab 3 — Risk register (a weakness proven exploitable and CONFIRMED raises the likelihood; a SINGLE row is flagged for verification); Lab 4 — Risk treatment and prevention plan (the recommendations set aside at step 3 are the starting point of the treatment options).

Nadia Roy has kept the May report in a drawer since June: “It says High three times. What exactly do I have to put in our risk list?” You answer with rows, each one traceable to a line of the report.

One report gives 27 rows: 7 software, 8 organizational, 8 human, 4 unknowns — and no material row. Fifteen rows are confirmed by a second source, seven rest on the report alone, and one is in conflict with the insurance questionnaire. The four positive observations are recorded as existing controls.

Code example 3 (Python) — Extract risk factors from the penetration test report

The task of this code

A Python script that reads PT-2026-05_report.txt and other_sources.csv, prints the identity and age of the report (step 1), turns each limitation into an UNKNOWN row (step 2), extracts every 'Weakness' and 'Contributing factor' line as one atomic fact with its line number (steps 3 and 4), proposes a resource category from the words of the sentence (step 5), corroborates each fact with the other sources (step 6) and writes pt_risk_factors.csv (step 7).

How it relates to the lecture and to the real-life example

The script performs the seven steps of Lesson 3 on Example 3. It never decides alone: the category is a proposal with the words that triggered it, and the analyst confirms or corrects it. The visualization highlights each line of the report as it is read and shows the row it produces.

kalmia_report_extractor.pystep 0
Execution window — the recorded output, step by step (pause to discuss a step)

The steps replayed above are the real output of the script, recorded when it was run on the course data on November 10, 2026 (Python 3 / PowerShell 7.4). Run it yourself from the downloaded folder to obtain the same result.

Step by step — what the code does

  1. The script imports csv, re (regular expressions) and date, fixes today's date to November 12, 2026, and defines RULES: an ordered list of (category, pattern) pairs. The first pattern found in a sentence proposes the category.
  2. TOPICS lists the words that identify a subject (password, MFA [multi-factor authentication], remote access, portal…). Two sentences that share a topic and an asset are compared during corroboration.
  3. propose_category() tries each rule in order with re.search, ignoring case, and returns the category and the matched words; if no rule matches, it returns TO REVIEW so that a person decides. topics_of() returns the topics of a sentence.
  4. main() reads the report into a list of lines (so each fact can cite its line number) and the other sources into a list of dictionaries, then prints [LOAD].
  5. Step 1 reads the header lines 'Key: value', converts the report date into a date, computes the age (167 days) and prints the identity, the authorization and the classification.
  6. The main loop reads the report line by line with enumerate(). A line 'L-n …' becomes an UNKNOWN row (step 2). A finding title starts a new finding. The 'Asset:' line sets the asset. The 'Recommendation:' line is attached to the facts of the finding and kept for Lab 4.
  7. Each 'Weakness:' or 'Contributing factor:' line becomes one atomic fact with an identifier such as PT-01-W1 or PT-01-C2, its asset, its line number and a proposed category with the words that justify it (steps 3 to 5). A 'P-n' line is recorded as an existing control.
  8. Step 6 compares each fact with the other sources about the same asset that share a topic: a contradicting source gives CONFLICT, at least one supporting source gives CONFIRMED, none gives SINGLE.
  9. Step 7 writes all rows to pt_risk_factors.csv with csv.DictWriter and prints the counts by category and by confidence: 7 software, 8 organizational, 8 human, 4 unknown; 15 confirmed, 7 single, 1 conflict.

Five flash-cards — click a card to reveal the answer

The four kinds of statements in a reportclick to reveal
Fact (becomes a risk factor), inference (verify first), recommendation (kept for Lab 4), limitation (recorded as an unknown).
The seven stepsclick to reveal
1 identify · 2 read the limits · 3 extract atomic facts · 4 translate · 5 classify · 6 corroborate · 7 record.
Risk factor statement patternclick to reveal
Asset or process — condition (source, location). One condition, verifiable, no solution inside, no likelihood or impact yet.
The four confidence levelsclick to reveal
CONFIRMED (two independent sources agree), SINGLE (one source), CONFLICT (sources disagree: record the conflict itself), UNKNOWN (not examined).
Severity versus riskclick to reveal
The report's severity rates the weakness in general; the risk level for Kalmia comes from likelihood and impact in Topic 5.

Self-check — 4 MCQs and 2 MSQs

Formative self-check — not evaluated. Quiz 3 (Monday, November 16) is a separate, evaluated quiz.
1. Which sentence from PT-2026-05 is a recommendation, and therefore must not be written as a risk factor? (MCQ — one answer)
  • ✕ This is a limitation: it becomes an unknown.
  • ✕ This is a fact describing an existing control.
  • ✓ Correct. It proposes an action; it is kept for the treatment plan of Lab 4.
  • ✕ This is a fact (a weakness) with evidence: it becomes a risk factor.
💡 Hint: A recommendation proposes an action.
2. Why do steps 1 and 2 (identify the document, read its limits) come before reading any finding? (MCQ — one answer)
  • ✕ Business owners are assigned by the organization in the risk factor list.
  • ✕ Limitations describe what was not examined.
  • ✓ Correct. A 167-day-old report, with ROAST-PC excluded, cannot be read as a description of November or of ROAST-PC.
  • ✕ Risk levels are decided in Topic 5, not taken from the summary.
💡 Hint: What could a reader forget if they started with the findings?
3. PT-05 states that the vendor's remote access has no MFA (multi-factor authentication); the insurance questionnaire CR-2026-01 declares MFA for all remote access. What does the analyst do? (MCQ — one answer)
  • ✓ Correct. The conflict is never settled by preference; Kalmia's declaration to its insurer is contradicted by its own evidence (KRF-23).
  • ✕ A signature does not make a declaration true; the test and the logs are stronger evidence.
  • ✕ Sources are not averaged; the disagreement is recorded.
  • ✕ Deleting hides the problem from the risk owner.
💡 Hint: A disagreement between sources is information.
4. Which statement follows the risk factor statement pattern correctly? (MCQ — one answer)
  • ✕ No verifiable condition, and the level of risk is decided later.
  • ✓ Correct: asset, one verifiable condition, source and location.
  • ✕ It blames a group without stating a verifiable condition.
  • ✕ This is a recommendation, not a condition.
💡 Hint: Asset or process — condition (source, location).
5. Which of the following are correct about the confidence levels used at step 6? (MSQ — select 4 answers)
  • ✓ Things not examined cannot be rated.
  • ✓ It is not deleted; it is flagged.
  • ✓ That is the definition.
  • ✕ The conflict is kept and becomes a risk factor of its own.
  • ✓ They are not independent.
  • ✕ Confidence describes the evidence, not the level of risk.
💡 Hint: Independence of the sources matters.
6. Which statements about extracting risk factors from PT-2026-05 are correct? (MSQ — select 4 answers)
  • ✓ They are the causes in the cause chain.
  • ✓ A penetration test looks for exploitable weaknesses; one source is never enough.
  • ✕ Severity is not risk.
  • ✓ They lower likelihood in Topic 5.
  • ✓ No owner or due date per finding: KRF-28.
  • ✕ They are checked against November evidence, not ignored.

Lesson 4 — Workshop: the list of risk factors for Kalmia

Rules of the list, consolidation of all sources, and the link to Lab 3
0:50 – 0:58

Read-aloud script — about 5 minutes

Professor cue Eight minutes to explain the workshop; the work itself happens in Hours 2 and 3. Show two merges on the board (FW-HQ portal; INC-04 + W-06) and one 'do not merge' case (the two NAS-01 conditions). Do not show the answer key before the teams finish their first pass.

The task of the workshop

In Hours 2 and 3 your team builds one consolidated risk factor list for Kalmia: a single table in which every condition found in any source appears once, with all its sources.

Your inputs are the three Class 6 lists (NA-, SW- and VS- rows), tonight's three outputs (resource_risk_factors.csv, source_register.csv, pt_risk_factors.csv) and the evidence pack. Your output is the list itself, saved in your course folder. Teams of three or four; twenty minutes for the first pass, then the comparison with the answer key.

The columns of the list

  • ID (identifier) — KRF-nn (Kalmia risk factor).
  • Asset or process — as named in the Lab 1 inventory.
  • Risk factor — the statement: one condition, verifiable.
  • Category — material, software, organizational or human.
  • Type — V (vulnerability) or PC (predisposing condition).
  • Sources — every document that shows the condition, with its location.
  • Confidence — CONFIRMED, SINGLE, CONFLICT or DOCUMENT (when the document itself is the evidence, as for a policy).
  • Business owner — the manager who decides about the asset (Nadia Roy, Karim Haddad or Sophie Tremblay), not the person who fixes it.
  • Question / unknown — what must still be verified.

The rules of consolidation

  1. One asset and one condition make one row. When two sources describe the same condition, merge them into one row and keep both sources. NA-16, PT-06 and MR-01 all describe the FW-HQ portal on the Internet: one row (KRF-12), three sources, confidence CONFIRMED.
  2. Never lose a source. A merged row lists every document that supports it; the confidence depends on it.
  3. At least three rows per category. The competency asks for the main risk factors of all four resource categories.
  4. Keep unknowns visible in their own short list: ROAST-PC never tested, café networks not covered, laptop encryption unknown, end-of-support dates missing, the Law 25 assessment of INC-04 not documented.
  5. No likelihood, no impact, no solution yet. Those belong to Lab 3 and Lab 4.
  6. Confidential. The list stays in your course folder (Legal Notice, s. 7.5).

From the workshop to Lab 3

On Saturday, Lab 3 — Risk register and prioritization — starts from this list. Each row will be linked to the threats of your Lab 2 catalogue, receive a likelihood and an impact on the Topic 5 scales, and take its place in the risk matrix and the risk register. A row without a source cannot be rated; a hidden unknown cannot be prioritized. That is why tonight's rules are strict.

The answer key below is the list our team of instructors built from the same evidence: 34 rows and 5 unknowns. Compare yours with it after your first pass, not before.

Key terms of this lesson

Consolidated risk factor list
One table in which each condition appears once, with all its sources.
Merge
Combining two or more statements that describe the same asset and the same condition into one row, keeping every source.
Business owner
The manager who decides about the asset and accepts or treats its risks; not the technician who fixes it.
Unknown
A part of the organization for which no current evidence exists; listed separately and kept visible.
Risk register
The table of risks with likelihood, impact, level, owner and treatment — built in Lab 3 from tonight's list.
Micro-activity — merge or not? (2 min)

Decide whether each pair must be merged into one row: (a) NA-16 'FW-HQ portal on the Internet (443)' and MR-01 '41,870 blocked logins on the FW-HQ portal'; (b) PT-01 'NAS (network-attached storage) admin password in acces.txt' and PT-01 'NAS web admin (HTTP [Hypertext Transfer Protocol] 5000) from any staff PC'; (c) W-06 'no offboarding checklist' and INC-04 'former supervisor exported 18,500 records'.

(a) Merge — same asset, same condition (exposed portal); the blocked attempts confirm it. (b) Do not merge — same asset, two conditions (a human practice and a software setting): two rows, linked. (c) Merge — the incident is evidence of the missing procedure; one organizational row (KRF-18) with both sources.

Code example 4 (self-contained HTML and JavaScript) — The workshop board

The task of this code

A single HTML (HyperText Markup Language) page that runs the consolidation step by step: it reads the 52 candidate statements one at a time, creates a new row in the right category column or merges the statement into an existing row (keeping its source), checks the workshop rules, lists the unknowns, shows the final 34-row table and exports it as a CSV (comma-separated values) file for Lab 3.

How it relates to the lecture and to the real-life example

The page performs the workshop of Lesson 4 in front of the class. Start/Pause, Step and Restart let the professor stop at any merge and ask why two statements are one row; the board, the counters and the execution window show the result of every decision.

kalmia_workshop_board.html — runs here; Start / Pause, Step and Restart are inside the page
The code of the page — a comment before every line (click to show or hide; use Copy code above)
Step by step — what the code does
  1. The head of the page holds the CSS rules: a sticky top bar with the controls, an inbox on the left, a board with four category columns, an execution window and a final table. No external file or library is loaded.
  2. The script starts with three data arrays written on one line each: KRF (the 34 rows of the answer key), CANDIDATES (the 52 statements, each with its source and the row it belongs to) and UNKNOWNS (the five unknowns).
  3. drawEmpty() writes one card per candidate in the inbox and four empty columns on the board; log() appends a line to the execution window; drawStats() recalculates the counters.
  4. step() performs one decision. In phase 1, it takes the next candidate, highlights it, and looks up the row it describes. If that row already exists, the statement is a duplicate: its source is added to the row, the card pulses, and a [MERGE] line explains why. Otherwise a new card is created in the column of its category and a [NEW] line is written.
  5. When all candidates are read, phase 2 checks the rules: every row has a source, each category has at least three rows, the single-source rows and the conflict are listed, and the five unknowns are printed.
  6. Phase 3 builds the final table with the merged sources of each row and writes a [DONE] line with the totals: 34 rows from 52 candidates, 18 duplicates merged.
  7. togglePlay() starts a timer that calls step() at the chosen speed, or stops it (pause); the Step button runs one decision; restart() resets the state and redraws the empty board.
  8. exportCsv() builds a CSV file with the columns of the list plus two empty columns, likelihood and impact, which Lab 3 will fill; a byte-order mark lets Excel read the accents.

The four resource categories
CategoryWhat must change?Typical evidenceUsual control type (Topic 6)
MaterialA physical item must be repaired, replaced or addedMonitoring reports (hardware health, UPS [uninterruptible power supply], temperature), incident reports, inventoryPhysical
SoftwareA program, firmware or a setting must changeScans, penetration tests, configuration reviews, monitoring (sign-in logs)Technical
OrganizationalA rule, document, role, contract or process must changePolicies and standards, contracts, compliance reports, incident root causesAdministrative
HumanWhat people know, do, or how many are available must changePhishing simulations, penetration tests (physical, social), interviews, HR (human resources) dataAdministrative (training, supervision)
The five internal information sources
Type of internal sourceWhat it revealsWhat it cannot revealKalmia documents
Penetration test reportWeaknesses proven exploitable; attack paths across categories; contributing causesAnything outside scope or time window; the organization's risk levelPT-2026-05
Compliance reportNonconformities with a law, standard or contract; declarations to third partiesProof of security (a 'compliant' answer is a declaration until verified)CR-2026-01, CR-2026-02
Incident reportConditions that already caused harm: root cause, contributing factors, lessons learnedWhat was never detectedIR-INC-01 to IR-INC-05
Network and host monitoring reportCurrent conditions: exposure, failures, hardware health, devices not reportingWhat the tool does not see; a report nobody reads protects nothingMR-01 to MR-05
Policies and standardsRules that exist, are outdated, unapproved or not appliedWhether people actually follow them (needs other evidence)PS-01, PS-02, PS-03
The seven-step reading method
StepNameWhat you do
1Identify the documentType, author, date, period, scope, authorization, classification; compute the age
2Read the limitsExclusions, time window, methods not used: each limit becomes an unknown
3Extract atomic factsOne condition per row, with its location
4TranslateAsset or process — condition (source, location)
5ClassifyCategory, vulnerability or predisposing condition, cause chain
6CorroborateSecond independent source → CONFIRMED / SINGLE / CONFLICT / UNKNOWN
7RecordID (identifier), references, category, confidence, business owner, open question; confidential
Confidence levels
LevelMeaningWhat to do
CONFIRMEDAt least two independent sources agreeKeep the row; cite all sources
SINGLEOne source onlyKeep the row; request a second source
CONFLICTSources disagreeRecord the conflict as a risk factor of its own
DOCUMENTThe document itself is the evidenceCite the document and its section
UNKNOWNNot examined by any current sourceList it separately; obtain evidence

reference
Official sites only, checked on November 10, 2026. Before opening a link, check it on VirusTotal (Legal Notice, s. 14.2 and Annex C) and, for an unknown domain, with Google Safe Browsing; a clean result is never a guarantee.
Course
  • Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice, Terms of Use and Acceptable Use Policy (v2.0) — The rules that govern these materials and every lab: authorization (s. 6.1), fictional data (s. 6.7), logs as personal information (s. 7.2), confidential findings and 'course work is not an audit' (s. 7.5), intrusion testing scope (s. 7.7.2), link safety (s. 14.2 and Annex C). (check on VirusTotal)

Standards and guides
  • NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-30 Rev. 1 — Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments — Defines risk factor, vulnerability and predisposing condition; Task 1-4 asks the assessor to identify the sources of threat, vulnerability and impact information. (check on VirusTotal)
  • NIST CSRC Glossary — risk factor — The official definition of risk factor used in Lesson 1. (check on VirusTotal)
  • NIST CSRC Glossary — predisposing condition — The official definition of predisposing condition used in Lesson 1. (check on VirusTotal)
  • NIST SP 800-115 — Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment — Penetration testing, its planning and its reporting (executive summary and detailed findings). (check on VirusTotal)
  • NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 — Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management — April 2025; links incident response and its lessons learned to cybersecurity risk management (a CSF [Cybersecurity Framework] 2.0 Community Profile). (check on VirusTotal)
  • NIST SP 800-92 — Guide to Computer Security Log Management — What logs are, why they must be reviewed, and how log management supports security. (check on VirusTotal)
  • NIST SP 800-137 — Information Security Continuous Monitoring — Monitoring as an ongoing source of information for risk decisions. (check on VirusTotal)
  • NIST SP 800-63B-4 — Authentication and Authenticator Management — Current guidance: verifiers shall not require periodic password changes; a change is forced only on evidence of compromise. (check on VirusTotal)
  • NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 — Governance, risk assessment (ID [identifier].RA) and continuous improvement from lessons learned. (check on VirusTotal)
  • ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27005:2022 — Guidance on managing information security risks — Risk identification; its examples of vulnerabilities are grouped by the type of asset that carries them. (check on VirusTotal)
  • ISO/IEC 27001:2022 — Information security management systems — Policies, roles, internal audit and corrective action in a management system. (check on VirusTotal)
  • CIS (Center for Internet Security) Critical Security Controls v8.1 — A prioritized set of safeguards used to compare a policy or a practice with an external standard. (check on VirusTotal)
  • PCI Security Standards Council — Publishes PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard), the security standard that merchants accepting payment cards must meet and confirm every year. (check on VirusTotal)
Canadian and Québec bodies
  • Canadian Centre for Cyber Security — Baseline cyber security controls for small and medium organizations — Thirteen baseline controls for organizations with fewer than 500 employees; used to compare Kalmia's documents with a Canadian reference. (check on VirusTotal)
  • Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (Cyber Centre) — Canada's technical authority on cyber security: guidance, alerts and advisories. (check on VirusTotal)
  • Get Cyber Safe (Government of Canada) — Awareness material that small organizations can use to train staff. (check on VirusTotal)
  • Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec (CAI [Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec]) — The body that oversees the Québec private-sector privacy law and receives notices of confidentiality incidents that present a risk of serious injury. (check on VirusTotal)

P-39.1) — The law amended by Law 25: person in charge (s. 3.1), governance policies (s. 3.2), privacy impact assessment (s. 3.3), notification (s. 3.5), confidentiality incident (s. 3.6), register (s. 3.8).
